title: The Mass (II.14)
hookLine: a fever, a newborn, a night shift: when the pew stays empty, Francis de Sales says you can still be there in heart
tomorrow: captain, student, granddaughter: does each need a different virtue?

lines: A FEVER. A NEWBORN. A NIGHT SHIFT.
CAN YOU BE THERE FROM BED?
cards: A fever. A newborn who finally fell asleep. A night shift that ends at dawn.
A car that won't start. Sunday comes, and the usual spot in the pew stays empty. For people who love the Mass, that can sting.
Francis de Sales wrote his chapter on the Mass for two readers at once: the one who walks in, and the one who can't. Can you be there from a bed? He says yes, and he says how.

teach.b: First, where the Mass stands. Among all the prayers in his book, Francis gives it a place of its own: the sun of spiritual exercises, the heart of devotion. Second, how to be there.
Go every day if you can, he says, so as to offer the sacrifice together with the priest. Third, how to pray through it.

He walks the Mass of his day in stages and pairs each one with a moment in the life of Jesus: asking pardon at the start, his coming and his life through the readings, his teaching with the Gospel and the Creed, then his passion and death, and at Communion, the desire to be one with him, ending in thanks.
Fourth, the reader who can't come. If you can't be there in body, he says, be there in heart. Choose a time, unite yourself in spirit with the Mass, and make your offering from wherever you are.
Catholic teaching today says the same kind of thing about Sunday.

teach.h: EACH PART, A MOMENT OF HIS LIFE.
teach.b: The Catechism asks the faithful to take part in Sunday Mass, and it names illness and the care of infants among the serious reasons that excuse.

teach.h: ABSENT IN BODY, PRESENT IN HEART.
teach.b: So for the one in bed, the door isn't shut.

how: Catholics take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days, and some go daily; those kept away by illness or caring for others often unite themselves with it in prayer, and some parishes bring them Communion.

games.q: your coworker's dad is in the hospital, and she'll be by his bed all Sunday morning. "guess I just miss it," she says. what does Francis offer her?
o: pick a time, unite herself in spirit with the Mass, and offer it from his bedside.
nothing; the Mass only reaches the people in the room.
she should leave him for an hour, since being there in person is all that counts.
games.why: if you can't be present in body, Francis says, be present in heart: choose a time and join the Mass in spirit from where you are.

practice: Sit up and rest your hands open on your knees, palms up, as if bringing something to an altar. Through the sit, stay with one part of the Mass you know, the Gospel, the Our Father, or Communion, and be there in spirit.
If you pray, join your own offering to it.

wordCard.voice: The Mass. For Francis, the center of the devout life's prayer: attended with care when you can, joined in spirit when you can't.

orig.note: Latin: the Mass, the word used in the Church's Latin liturgy.

carryVoice: The line to keep: join it, from the pew or from wherever the day finds you. Be well.
